title: “Is It Sin to Enjoy Sex… or Only to Abuse It?”
paragraphs:
“Is It Sin to Enjoy Sex… or Only to Abuse It?”
The question nobody says out loud… but everyone is silently wrestling with.
It usually doesn’t start with rebellion.
It starts with confusion.
A quiet question sitting in the back of your mind while you scroll, while you remember, while you feel something you don’t know how to categorize anymore…
“Why do I feel guilty… for something God created?”
And you don’t say it out loud, because in church circles, even asking the question can feel dangerous.
But let’s be honest for a second—really honest.
Somewhere along the way, many believers were taught to associate desire with shame… intimacy with suspicion… and pleasure with sin.
So now you’re stuck in this silent tension—wanting to honor God, but also wondering why something that feels so natural feels so condemned.
And if you’ve ever asked yourself that question… you’re not alone.
But more importantly—Scripture actually answers it.
Not with cultural opinions… not with fear-based control… but with truth.
Raw, unfiltered, and deeply freeing truth.
Because when God first designed intimacy, He didn’t whisper it in shame.
He spoke it boldly in blessing.
In the beginning, before sin ever entered the world, before guilt distorted what was pure, there was this moment in Genesis that most people rush past without realizing how profound it is:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
(Vayihyu sheneihem arummim ha’adam ve’ishto velo yitboshashu)
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25)
No shame.
No guilt.
No confusion.
Just purity.
Just design.
Just union exactly the way God intended it.
Let that settle for a moment.
Before sin corrupted the human heart, intimacy was not hidden… it was holy.
So what changed?
Not the design.
The distortion.
Sin didn’t create sex—it corrupted it.
Which means the issue was never enjoyment.
The issue was always misuse.
That’s why Scripture never condemns intimacy within God’s design—it celebrates it.
Read this slowly, without rushing past it:

“דּוֹדִי לִי וַאֲנִי לוֹ”
(Dodi li va’ani lo)
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” (Song of Songs 2:16)
That entire book—often avoided—is a poetic, God-preserved expression of desire, affection, longing, and physical attraction within covenant love.
Not tolerated.
Celebrated.
Even in the New Testament, Paul doesn’t command distance in marriage—he commands connection:

“μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους…”
(Mē apostereite allēlous)
“Do not deprive one another…” (1 Corinthians 7:5)
That’s not restriction.
That’s protection.
That’s God saying: intimacy, when kept inside covenant, is not something to fear—it’s something to steward.
So no… enjoying intimacy itself is not sin.
But abusing it?
Twisting it?
Removing it from God’s design?
That’s where the fracture begins.
Because outside of God’s order, what was meant to unite begins to wound.
What was meant to give life begins to take it.
What was meant to reflect covenant becomes driven by consumption.
And that’s the part no one tells you plainly.
The problem isn’t that you feel desire.
The problem is when desire becomes detached from truth.
Jesus didn’t come to erase desire—He came to restore it.
Because even the word “lust” in Scripture carries a deeper meaning than just attraction.
“ἐπιθυμέω” (epithumeō)—to crave, to set your heart upon, to long for something in a way that takes rather than gives.
That’s the difference.
Holy desire gives.
Sinful desire consumes.
One reflects love.
The other reflects hunger without covenant.
And if we’re being real… a lot of people aren’t struggling because they enjoy intimacy.
They’re struggling because they’ve been taught to feel ashamed of something God created, while simultaneously being surrounded by a world that abuses it in every direction.
That confusion creates silence.
That silence creates hidden battles.
And hidden battles grow into quiet shame.
But Jesus never approached brokenness with shame.
He approached it with truth and restoration.
Think about the woman caught in adultery.
Exposed.
Condemned.
Ready to be destroyed.
And yet Jesus didn’t say, “Your desire is the problem.”
He said, “Go and sin no more.”
He addressed the misuse… not the existence of longing.
Because He knew something we often forget—
The goal isn’t suppression.
It’s transformation.
And that changes everything.
Because suddenly, you realize…
God isn’t trying to take something from you.
He’s trying to protect something sacred.
He’s not anti-pleasure.
He’s anti-destruction.
Sit in it.
Because some of you have been carrying shame that God never placed on you.
And others of you know… you’ve crossed lines that you can’t pretend didn’t happen.
Both need the same thing.
Grace.
Real grace.
The kind that doesn’t ignore truth—but meets you inside it.
Because the Gospel was never about pretending we’re clean.
It was about Jesus making us clean.
And this is where everything shifts.
From scandal… to grace.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don’t brush it off.
Be honest.
Let it be real.
Let it be seen.
Because healing grows where honesty lives.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this… someone struggling, confused, or silently battling—don’t keep this to yourself.
Not to expose them—but to reach them.
You never know who’s been waiting for truth like this.
Because there will be moments when your mind gets loud again… and you’ll need to come back to what God actually said.
Stay close to truth.
Because drifting is subtle… but so is growth.
And for those who want to go deeper—not just reading but truly growing—there’s something waiting for you.
Not surface-level content.
Real spiritual nourishment.
If your heart is in this… if you want to glorify God not just in words but in action… then stand with us.
Not out of pressure.
But out of purpose.
Because when truth reaches you… it’s meant to reach others through you.
And maybe this is the moment where something changes.
Not just what you believe…
But how you live.
Because what God made holy was never meant to feel dirty—only restored.
